title: How Shazam finds a song in a loud bar
description:
Shazam turns a few seconds of sound into a spectrogram (time across, pitch up), keeps only the loudest points, a 'constellation' of stars, and pairs each star with about 10 stars just after it. Each pair (two pitches plus the time gap, 30 bits) is one pattern in about a billion, so a lookup is fast and specific. The right song is the one whose matching pairs all agree on the same moment in the track, so even when only 1 or 2 pairs in 100 survive the noise, it still wins. In the 2003 paper, 10-second clips were still recognised half the time with pub noise 4 times louder than the music.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py), including a toy version of the search on 1,000 random songs. Source: Avery Li-Chun Wang, An Industrial-Strength Audio Search Algorithm (ISMIR 2003).

The math behind real problems, twice a day. Subscribe and the next one finds you.

social_caption: Shazam can name a song even when the bar is louder than the music. It turns sound into a map of stars and matches pairs of them.
facts_checked: Spectrogram peaks = constellation map; 1024 frequency bins = at most 10 bits per peak; anchors paired with points in a target zone, fan-out F = 10; a pair = two frequencies + time gap = 30 bits (2^30 = 1.07 billion), about a million times more specific (2^20); hashes packed in 32 bits (https://www.ee.columbia.edu/~dpwe/papers/Wang03-shazam.pdf, fetched 2026-11-27)
Right track: matching hashes line up at one time offset (histogram peak); from a heavily corrupted 15 s sample a match with only about 1-2% of hash tokens surviving (same paper, sec. 2.3 and 3.1)
50% recognition at about -9, -6, -3 dB SNR for 15, 10, 5 s clips with pub noise (paper, sec. 3.1): -6 dB = noise power 3.98x the music (verify.py)
CTA: half the stars survive -> a pair needs both -> 1 in 4 (paper: pair survival ~ p^2); simulated 200,000 trials: 0.249 (verify.py)

Toy search (verify.py): 1,000 random 3-minute star maps, 10 s clips keeping 40% of stars plus 3 noise stars per real one: 1.4% of the clip's pairs survive, 300 of 300 clips found the right song (median score 45 vs best wrong 3)

beats.say: Shazam finds your song even when the noise is louder than the music.
It doesn't listen to the tune. It throws away almost all the sound.
It gets a few noisy seconds from your phone, and millions of songs to check.
First, turn the sound into a picture. Time across, pitch up the side.
Now keep only the loudest points. Your song becomes a map of stars. The noise adds stars, but the song's loudest ones mostly survive.
But one star means almost nothing. It's just a pitch, one of 1,024.
So pair each star with the 10 stars right after it. Two pitches plus the gap between them: one pattern in a billion.
Look up every pair. Each hit says: this song, this second.
Wrong songs get random hits. The right song's hits all point to the same moment.
So only 1 or 2 pairs in 100 have to survive the noise. That's how your phone names a song in a loud bar.
If half the stars survive, how many pairs survive? Tell me in the comments.
